section_summary: This section contains documents from late 1935 to mid-1937 concerning Japanese foreign relations, domestic politics, economic planning, and demographics. It features Japanese Foreign Office and organizational publications—namely a bilingual compilation of articles by Colonel Edward M. House and Prince Fumimaro Konoe advocating the redistribution of colonial territories and raw materials, and an address by Ambassador Naotake Sato analyzing population growth, industrialization, and export competition. It also includes U.S. State Department despatches and memoranda examining the Hayashi Cabinet's proposed establishment of a central Planning Board (Kikakucho) and reporting on the April 30, 1937 general election, which saw substantial gains for the Social Mass Party alongside the government's continued resistance to traditional party rule.

subfiles.about: A Japanese Foreign Office publication presenting articles by Colonel Edward M. House and Prince Fumimaro Konoe on colonial and economic readjustment to prevent international conflict.
subfiles.summary: This bilingual bulletin issued by the Information Bureau of the Japanese Foreign Ministry (Gaimusho), published as Kokusai Jijo No. 464, contains Japanese translations and original English texts of articles by American statesman Colonel Edward M. House and House of Peers President Prince Fumimaro Konoe originally published in Liberty magazine. House advocates an international 'new deal' in which the satisfied powers (the United States, Great Britain, France, and Russia) share colonial territories, raw materials, and economic opportunities with have-not nations (Germany, Italy, and Japan) to avoid catastrophic conflicts. Konoe strongly endorses House's thesis, arguing that dynamic but resource-poor nations are unfairly constrained by the existing status quo and that lasting peace requires an equitable distribution of land and resources rather than rigid collective security through the League of Nations.
subfiles.title: Kokusai Jijo No. 464: Ryodo oyobi Shigen Sai-chosei Ron (On the Readjustment of Territory and Resources)

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing reports on the Japanese Cabinet's approval of a proposed Planning Board (Kikakucho).
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (William T. Turner)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs reports that the Japanese Cabinet has approved the establishment of a comprehensive Planning Board (Kikakucho) incorporating the existing Cabinet Inquiry Bureau. The memorandum notes that the board is designed to meet the demands of a planned economy and reflects military pressure for administrative reform dating back to the February 26 Incident of 1936. While the Embassy notes speculation regarding whether the board might serve as a central organ for a future fascist government, FE concludes that detailed speculation regarding its powers and personnel is premature until official decisions are enacted.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Proposed Japanese Planning Board

subfiles.about: An American Embassy despatch reporting on Cabinet approval of the Kikakucho (Planning Board) and enclosing a press report on its structure and prospective personnel.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that the Hayashi Cabinet has approved the creation of a Planning Board (Kikakucho) incorporating the Cabinet Inquiry Bureau to coordinate national legislation, state policies, and economic planning. Grew views the initiative as an outcome of Premier Hayashi's conviction that traditional political institutions cannot manage modern national leadership, though it remains uncertain whether it represents a stepping stone toward fascist governance. An enclosed clipping from The Japan Advertiser of April 20, 1937, details the board's organizational framework, concurrent presidency under Finance Minister Toyotaro Yuki, a concurrent Central Economic Council, and prominent business and political leaders suggested as members.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2395: Proposed Japanese Planning Board

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 2402 concerning the Japanese general election of April 30, 1937.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (William T. Turner)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Ambassador Grew's initial report on the April 30 Japanese general election, highlighting voter apathy reflected in a forty percent abstention rate. It notes Finance Minister Toyotaro Yuki's declaration that the government plans to assist in organizing a new party of like-minded men and will dissolve the Diet again if necessary. The memorandum agrees with the Embassy's assessment that the Hayashi Cabinet is determined to prevent a return to the pre-1932 party system of government.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on First Report on Japanese Elections

subfiles.about: An American Embassy despatch reporting on the April 30, 1937 Japanese general election, the advance of the Social Mass Party, and the Hayashi Cabinet's political strategy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits preliminary results and press clippings from the April 30, 1937 Japanese general election, noting significant voter apathy and a 40 percent abstention rate during a colorless campaign focused merely on clean elections. Despite the Hayashi Cabinet's efforts to discipline the Diet through dissolution, the established opposition parties (Minseito and Seiyukai) maintained their majority, while the proletarian Social Mass Party (Shakai Taishuto) scored substantial gains, especially in Tokyo. Finance Minister Toyotaro Yuki stated that the government will sponsor a new political party and would not hesitate to dissolve the Diet again, underscoring its determination to prevent a return to parliamentary party government. Three enclosed clippings from The Japan Advertiser provide detailed election returns, an interview with Prince Fumimaro Konoe questioning Hayashi's dissolution strategy, and an editorial analyzing the Cabinet's post-election options.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2402: First Report on Japanese Elections

subfiles.about: A published bilingual lecture by Japanese Ambassador Naotake Sato analyzing Japan's population growth, industrialization, and foreign trade expansion.
subfiles.summary: This bilingual English-French pamphlet publishes an address delivered on January 27, 1936, by Naotake Sato, Japanese Ambassador to France, before the Centre d'Études de Politique Étrangère in Paris, presided over by André Siegfried. Sato analyzes Japan's rapid demographic growth, high population density per square kilometer of arable land, and the annual influx of hundreds of thousands of workers into the labor market. Citing demographic research by Professor Teijiro Ueda and economic studies by Fernand Maurette and Professor T. E. Gregory, Sato argues that birth control and emigration cannot solve Japan's immediate economic dilemma. Instead, Japan must rely on industrialization, rationalization of production, and expanding manufactured exports, refuting Western allegations of 'social dumping' and demonstrating that Japanese exports represent only a modest share of global trade.
subfiles.title: The Problem of Population and Industrialisation in Japan (Le Problème de la population et l'industrialisation du Japon)
